summary: This version of the library program builds a Map that links each book's title to the Book object itself, so a book can be found by name instead of by scanning the whole list. It then looks up "The Hobbit" and prints its details, or a not-found message when the title is missing.

lines.text: Map is the interface for a collection of key-value pairs; you program against this type so the concrete implementation can change later.
HashMap is the everyday implementation of Map, offering fast lookups by key with no guaranteed ordering.
The list is the master copy of the collection; the map built below is just an index into these same objects.
The key type is String (the title) and the value type is Book, so one lookup returns the whole object rather than a single field.
Walking the list once is what fills the index; after this loop the map does the searching for you.
put stores the book under its own title, and because keys are unique a duplicate title would overwrite the earlier entry.
Holding the search term in a variable keeps it out of the lookup and the messages, so it only has to be changed in one place.
get returns the matching Book, or null when no entry exists for that key — a map never throws for a missing key.
Because get can hand back null, this null check must come before any method is called on foundBook.
Concatenating the object into a string calls its toString method, which is why Book defines one.
With the whole object in hand, any of its fields can be read — an advantage over a map that stored only the author's name.
The else branch reports the absence of a title, which is friendlier than letting a null slip further into the program.
